pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written nnw; conventionally vocalised “Nun”. The name is the primeval water itself.
The waters of chaos from which the first mound rose; grammatically masculine here, feminine as Naunet.

pronunciation.note: Every creation cosmogony begins in Nun; every flood-season re-enacts it.

domains.title: God of the Primeval Waters
domains.subtitle: The Inert One, the Flood Before the World
domains.lead: Nnw — Nun — is not a god of things but of the nothing before things: the dark, inert, life-teeming water that existed before creation and surrounds the world still. Every cosmogony begins in him; every temple’s holy lake is his miniature; and every year the Nile’s flood re-stages his one eternal act — potential flooding into form.

cards.name: The Primeval Water
cards.desc: The chaos-flood from which the first mound — and every creator — emerged.

cards.name: Bearer of the Mound
cards.desc: He lifts the ben-ben: the primeval hill on which the creator stood to speak the world.

cards.name: The Ogdoad Pair
cards.desc: With Naunet he heads the eight frog- and snake-headed forces of primordial inertness.

cards.name: Surrounding Ocean
cards.desc: The world floats in him as a bubble in a flood; beyond the horizon, Nun resumes.

mythology.lead: Nun’s mythology is Egypt’s creation mythology seen from the water’s side. He never acts — that is his nature, and the meaning of his name, ‘the inert one’ — but everything that acts, acts upon or out of him. The creator gods of every temple city are alike in one thing: they stood on Nun’s surface and spoke.

myths.title: The Ogdoad and the First Mound
myths.text: At Hermopolis the theology ran: four frog-headed males and four snake-headed females — Nun and Naunet, Huh and Hauhet, Kuk and Kauket, Amun and Amaunet — swam in the primordial water until their inertness ripened into an egg, or a lotus, or the first mound. From that the sun rose. Nun heads the eight because water is first among the inert things.

myths.title: The Word Upon the Waters
myths.text: The Shabaka Stone’s Memphite account has Ptah conceiving the world in the heart and speaking it on the primeval waters: creation as a command uttered over Nun. The theology made the water the page and the god’s tongue the pen — the deepest Egyptian metaphor for creation as articulation.

myths.title: The Sea That Holds the Barque
myths.text: In the underworld books the sun’s night barque sails the Nun beneath the world — the primeval water is also the water below, the source of renewal. At dawn the barque re-emerges from Nun’s eastern flood: every sunrise is a re-creation, every night a return to the uncreated.

myths.title: The Inundation as Epiphany
myths.text: The Egyptians called the annual flood simply ‘the arrival’; its waters were Nun revisiting the world, refertilising the mound. Temple holy lakes and the ‘Ocean of the Temple’ pools staged the same theology in architecture: a miniature primeval water at the god’s door, in which purity and creation are the same act.

lore.syncretism: Nun is the substrate into which every creator-god’s theology sinks its roots: Atum self-created upon him, Amun hidden within him, Ptah speaking over him. In the late period he was invoked as ‘father of the gods’ while remaining, strictly, no-one’s child. Greek cosmologists drew the parallel with their own water-first doxographies — Thales’ ‘all is water’ found its Egyptian precedent in Nun.
lore.culturalLegacy: The image of the world as a bubble of order in an infinite flood passed from Egyptian cosmogony into Hermetic and Gnostic speculation about the deep; and the Nile flood as ‘the return of the uncreated’ remains one of the most quoted ideas in Egyptological writing on time and renewal.
lore.extendedMeditation: Nun is the shortest name with the largest referent in the entire lexicon: the water before names. To write him in ASCII is almost redundant — his element needs no spelling, only sounding. Read the name aloud and you have performed his nature: the open vowel, the held n, the open vowel again — a breathing in and out, the flood arriving and withdrawing.

sources.name: Amduat and Book of Gates (the night water)
Bonneau, La crue du Nil (flood theology)

lore.archaeology: No temple was exclusively Nun’s — water has no address — but every temple carried him: holy lakes, ‘ocean’ basins, and the primeval-mound imagery of the sanctuary floor. The Ogdoad’s frog and snake figures crowd the Late Period faience amulets found across Egypt.
lore.cult: His cult was enacted rather than addressed: the flood’s arrival, the temple lake’s stillness, the purity-ablutions of every priest at dawn. Hymns call him ‘father who revived himself’ — the water that needs no cult because it is the condition of all cult.
lore.iconography: A man waist-deep in water, arms raised to lift the solar barque or the mound — the ḥꜣ gesture of uplift; or one of the Ogdoad’s frog-heads in profile. His hieroglyph is three rippling lines: the same sign that writes water everywhere in the language.
lore.reception: Greek doxographers listed Nun among the ‘Egyptian first-principles’, and the comparison with Thales became a commonplace of ancient philosophy’s self-history. Modern cosmology has its own echo: the quantum vacuum, the sea of potential from which the universe’s mound arose, reads uncannily like Nun re-described in mathematics.
